Lecture 7 Notes

Quantitative Data Analysis

Introduction

  • Last time, we met the idea of testing whether observed differences were due to sampling error

  • We tested for differences between average male and average female wages

  • Today we will learn how to test for differences between more than two categories

  • Let’s see whether the average wage varies by education level (measured as the highest qualification a person has obtained)

  • For all our sake, let’s hope so!

Level of highest qualification

Highest Qualification Obs. Mean Wage (£) Std. Dev.
Degree or equivalent 3535 25.02 12.65
Higher education 565 19.63 9.88
A level or equivalent 1604 17.33 8.86

No Qualification 210 13.53 5.39

Level of highest qualification

Education

  • We can see from the chart that the median wage varies with education

  • There is, however, substantial overlap

  • If we drew a new sample, would the differences be reproduced

What is our hypothesis?

  • We think education and wages are related \[H_0: \mu_{degree} = \mu_{HE} = \mu_{A level} = \mu_{GCSE} = \mu_{Other} = \mu_{None}\] \[H_A: \mu_{degree} \neq \mu_{HE} \neq \mu_{A level} \neq \mu_{GCSE} \neq \mu_{Other} \neq \mu_{None}\]

The linear model

  • We can use framework of the linear model to write down an equation

  • Define a set of dummy variables which take the value if:

    • One if the qualification in question is the highest the person possesses
    • Zero otherwise

The regression equation

\[\textrm{Wage}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \textrm{HE}_i + \beta_2 \cdot \textrm{A level}_i + \beta_3 \cdot \textrm{GCSE}_i + \\ \beta_4 \cdot \textrm{Other}_i + \beta_5 \cdot \textrm{None}_i\]

The parameters

  • \(\beta_0\) will be the average wage of a person with a degree

  • \(\beta_1\) is the difference between the average wage of a person with a degree and a person with only some higher education

  • \(\beta_2\) is the difference between the average wage of a person with a degree and a person with A levels

  • \(\beta_3\) is the difference between the average wage of a person with a degree and a person with GCSEs

  • \(\beta_4\) is the difference between the average wage of a person with a degree and a person with some other qualification

  • \(\beta_5\) is the difference between the average wage of a person with a degree and a person with no qualifications

The linear regression model

lm(HOURPAY ~ HIQUL22D, data = lfs) %>% summary()

The linear regression model

Interpretation

  • We have some strong results here

  • Every level of education below degree has a lower wage on average

  • All of the differences are statistically significant

  • In this case, we have enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis we set up earlier

  • However, this might not always be the case

  • We may find instances where nothing is individually significant, but the parameters are jointly significant

Variation

  • Variation in the data can occur along two dimensions

    1. Within a group (within an education category)
    2. Between groups (between education categories)

  • The question we need to answer is whether the variation between groups is significantly greater than the variation from person to person

Formalising these concepts

  • We need to formalise the concepts of variation we have discussed:

    1. Total variation: the sum of squares total (SST)
    2. Among-group variation: sum of squares among groups (SSA)
    3. Within-group variation: sum of squares within groups (SSW)

Total variation

We can define the sum of squares total as:

\[SST = \sum_{j=1}^c{\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}{(X_{ij}-\bar{\bar{X}})^2}}\] where

  • \(\bar{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^c{\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}{X_{ij}}}}{n} =\) Grand Mean
  • \(X_{ij}\) is the \(i\)th value in group \(j\)
  • \(n_j\) is the number of values in group \(j\)
  • \(n\) is the total number of values across all groups
  • \(c\) is the number of groups

Among-group variation

We define the among group variation as:

\[SSA=\sum_{j=1}^c{n_j(\bar{X}_j - \bar{\bar{X}})^2}\]

where

  • \(c\) is the number of groups
  • \(n_j\) is the number of values in group \(j\)
  • \(\bar{X}_j\) is the sample mean of group \(j\)
  • \(\bar{\bar{X}}\) is the grand mean

Within-group variation

We define the within-group variation as:

\[SSW = \sum_{j=1}^c{\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}{(X_{ij}-\bar{X}_j)^2}}\] where

  • \(X_{ij}\) is the \(i\)th value in group \(j\)
  • \(\bar{X}_j\) is the sample mean of group \(j\)

Mean squares

  • We can convert these three sums of squares (SS) into variances or mean squares by dividing them by their degrees of freedom (d.o.f.)

    1. The among-group SS compares \(c\) groups and contributes \(c-1\) d.o.f.
    2. Since each of the \(c\) groups contributes \(n_j-1\) d.o.f. , there are \(n-c\) d.o.f. associated with the within-group SS
    3. The total variation contributes \(n-1\) d.o.f. since we have \(n\) values and \(1\) grand mean

The Mean Square Errors

The Mean Square Among:

\[MSA = \frac{SSA}{c-1}\] The Mean Square Within:

\[MSW = \frac{SSW}{n-c}\] The Mean Square Total:

\[MST = \frac{SST}{n-1}\]

Testing

  • To conduct our test we need to:

    1. State our null and alternative hypotheses
    2. Define our test statistic
    3. Choose a level of significance

Hypotheses

\[H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = ... = \mu_c\] \[H_A: \mu_1 \neq \mu_2 \neq ... \neq \mu_c\]

  • The null hypothesis states that the means for each group are not statistically different from each other

  • The alternative states that not all of the means are equal

  • It may be that only 1 mean is statistically significantly different from the others

  • The method will not tell us which mean(s) is(are) different

The test statistic

  • To test our null hypothesis, we use an F-test

  • This makes use of an F-distribution

\[F=\frac{MSA}{MSW}\]

  • \(F\) is our test statistic with \(c-1\) degrees of freedom on the numerator and \(n-c\) degrees of freedom on the denominator
  • MSA is the Mean Square Among
  • MSW is the Mean Square Within

The F-test

  • Mercifully we don’t have to calculate it all by hand

  • We can ask R to do it using the analysis of variance (ANOVA) function

aov(HOURPAY ~ HIQUL22D, data = lfs) %>% summary()
##               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)    
## HIQUL22D       5 126542   25308   218.1 <2e-16 ***
## Residuals   7341 851935     116                   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Interpretation

  • You can see that R gives us some details of the underlying calculations

  • It tells us the final F value

  • Crucially we get the p-value

  • It is well below zero so we can safely reject our null hypothesis

  • It seems the average wage varies with education level

Additional information

  • Note that the Sum Sq column presents the sum of squares

  • This is a measure of the variation in the data

  • It is broken into two components

    1. Variation attributable to our categorical variable (HIQUL22D)
    2. Variation which we have failed to explain (Residuals)

  • From this we can calculate how much variation is explained by our education variable

  • We divide the sum of squares from HIQUL22D by the total sum of squares

\[\frac{126542}{126542 + 851935} = 0.129325\]

Interpretation

  • This value comes to 0.129325

  • It indicates that education levels explain about 12.93% of the variation in wage levels

  • With all this in mind, let us return to our linear model from the start of the lecture

The linear model

  • We have now seen some of the magic of the linear model

  • An assumption of the model is that the dependent variable is interval/ratio

  • We have seen how categorical variables can be included as independent variables

  • Ordinal variables work in the same way, expect that the model doesn’t utilise their ordinal nature

  • We can also have an interval/ratio variable as an independent variable

  • Suppose we want to know about age and earnings

Measuring a relationship

  • Visualising the data is an important step in understanding the relationship between two variables

  • It is also useful to be able to quantify the relationship between two variables

  • This step will also be necessary if we want to test for statistical significance

  • There are several ways we can do this

Variance

  • We have met the idea of variance in reference to one variable

  • We can look at how two variables co-vary

  • Recall that the sample variance is given as:

\[S_x^2 = \frac{\sum_i^n (x_i-\bar{x})^2}{n-1} \] - The sample covariance is given by:

\[ \textrm{cov}(X,Y)=\sum_{i=1}^N{\frac{(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{n-1}}\]

Covariance

  • If when \(x\) is above its mean, \(y\) is above its mean, the covariance is positive

  • If when \(x\) is below its mean, \(y\) is above its mean, the covariance is negative

  • If \(x\) moving tells us nothing about what is happening with \(y\), the covariance is zero

  • The units are hard to interpret because they depend on the units of \(x\) and \(y\)

  • A standard approach is to normalise it by the product of the individual variances

  • This gives the so-called Pearson product moment correlation coefficient, a measure bound between -1 and 1

\[r= \frac{\sum{(x-\bar{x})(y-\bar{y}})} {\sqrt{\sum{(x-\bar{x})^2} \sum{(y-\bar{y})^2}}}\]

Interpreting the absolute value of r

Range Relative strength
0 No relationship
0-0.2 Very weak, negligible relationship
0.2-0.4 Weak, low association
0.4-0.7 Moderate association
0.7-0.9 Strong, high, marked association
0.9-1 Very high, very strong relationship
1 Perfect association

Getting a correlatoin coefficient in R

  • To get just the correlation coefficient we can use the cor() function
cor(lfs$HOURPAY, lfs$AGE)
## [1] 0.1375462

Testing statistical significance

  • We can use the cor.test() function to test the statistical significance of the correlation
cor.test(lfs$HOURPAY, lfs$AGE)
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  lfs$HOURPAY and lfs$AGE
## t = 11.901, df = 7345, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.1150412 0.1599101
## sample estimates:
##       cor 
## 0.1375462

Testing statistical significance

  • We can get the same thing using formula notation
cor.test(~ HOURPAY + AGE, data=lfs)
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  HOURPAY and AGE
## t = 11.901, df = 7345, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.1150412 0.1599101
## sample estimates:
##       cor 
## 0.1375462

The linear model

  • We can’t see the correlation coefficient directly here, but it is here

  • If we take the square root of the \(R^2\), then we get the correlation coefficient

  • In this case, it happens that the Estimate is also close to the correlation coefficient

  • This is a coincidence, although the two measures are related

  • Let’s first find out where it comes from

Guessing a person’s wage

  • If I draw a random person from the population and ask you to guess their wage, your best guess will be the mean
## Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
## ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.
## This warning is displayed once every 8 hours.
## Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
## generated.

A better guess

  • We can see that younger people have lower wages

  • If we knew a person’s age, we could make a better prediction of their wage

  • Currently, our guess is given by the equation \(\textrm{HOURPAY}_i = \beta_0\)

  • Let’s add age into our equation \(\textrm{HOURPAY}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\cdot\textrm{AGE}\)

  • This isn’t quite right, because we can’t pick values for \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) which would perfectly predict wages

  • Let’s add a term to capture our error: \(\textrm{HOURPAY}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\cdot\textrm{AGE} + \varepsilon_i\)

Selecting parameters

  • The task is to select values for \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) which optimise our guess

  • Our \(\varepsilon\) term captures how wrong we are i.e., the residual

  • We want to minimise how wrong we are

  • We can capture a metric of how wrong we are by summing the square of our residuals i.e., \(\textrm{SSR} = \sum\varepsilon_i^2\)

  • Now we select values which will minimise this

  • We could solve the problem numerically

  • We can also use calculus

Equations to solve

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial \hat{\beta_0}} \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1}x_i)^2 = -2 \sum{(y_i-\hat{\beta_0}-\hat{\beta_1}x_i)}\]

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial \hat{\beta_1}} \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1}x_i)^2 = -2 \sum{x_i(y_i-\hat{\beta_0}-\hat{\beta_1}x_i)}\]

The solution

\[\hat{\beta_1}=\frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i y_i - \bar{x}\bar{y}}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2-\bar{x}^2}\]

\[\hat{\beta_0}=\bar{y}-\hat{\beta_1}\bar{x}\]

The linear model

  • We have already seen the solution for these parameters

  • \(\beta_0\) is the intercept from the linear model

  • \(\beta_1\) is the coefficient attached to age

  • We can visualise what this looks like

The linear model

lm(HOURPAY ~ AGE, data=lfs) %>% summary()
##

## lm(formula = HOURPAY ~ AGE, data = lfs)

Interpretation

  • The intercept tells us the wage of a person who is zero years old

  • This isn’t a helpful interpretation

  • In the linear model, we don’t generally bother interpreting the intercept

  • The coefficient attached to age tells us the association between age and wage

  • Being a year older is associated with wages which are £0.13 higher

  • The effect is statistically significant

  • Variation in age accounts for 1.9% of variation in wages

Correlation and causation

Correlation is not causation

Cum hoc ergo propter hoc

  • This is a well known logical fallacy

  • All we show with these methods is an association

  • We must be careful when writing up this kind of analysis

  • Do not talk about proving things

  • Do not talk about things causing things

  • Talk about things being associated with other things

Summary

  • We have seen some more of the magic of the linear model

  • It can measure associations using categorical, ordinal and scale/interval independent variables

  • It can test for statistical significance

  • There are yet more wonders to behold
